item.title: As Serbian student movement ends ruling party’s 12-year reign, here are the challenges they face
item.description: The Student List has no standalone leader and fielded candidates without political experience from across Serbian society.
item.content:encoded:
Serbia’s student-led political movement has secured a historic election victory. Preliminary results suggest the so-called Student List has won 141 of the 250 seats in parliament, with the ruling Serbian Progressive Party taking 104. The result brings the 12-year rule of Alexander Vučić to an end.

The Student List’s story is remarkable. It has no standalone leader and fielded candidates without political experience from across Serbian society. Stemming from student-led protests against the entrenched corruption and creeping authoritarianism of the ruling regime, it has now achieved an improbable dream.

In late 2025, one of us (Gavin Brent Sullivan) conducted focus groups with members of the student protest movement as part of the Pledge EU Horizon project. The project explores the emotional dynamics of political grievances and their democratic implications.

The protesters’ grievances were centred on the 2024 collapse of a roof at the newly renovated Novi Sad train station in northern Serbia, which killed 16 people. Allegations of state involvement through corruption in the procurement process and lowered building standards have been denied by the government. But they nonetheless sparked large nationwide protests.

item.title: Why more people are resorting to ‘DIY’ health advice and it is dangerous
item.description: Online searches may occasionally point people in the right direction, but they can also encourage unnecessary anxiety or false reassurance.
item.content:encoded:
Need treatment fast? Many people now turn to Google before a healthcare professional. From checking symptoms online to buying medicines online and taking advice from social media influencers, healthcare is increasingly becoming a do-it-yourself activity.

Convenience is a big part of the appeal. Information is available instantly – no need to wait weeks to see a GP – and online communities often provide reassurance from people with similar experiences.

Researching a health problem on the internet can feel empowering. But while greater access to health information has benefits, the rise of DIY healthcare also comes with risks. Research suggests that diagnosing and treating yourself, or relying on unqualified sources for advice, can lead to mistakes, the wrong use of medicines and delays in getting professional help.

The internet has changed the way people access health information. A few decades ago, someone worried about a symptom might consult a doctor, pharmacist or medical reference book. Today, a search engine can generate thousands of results in seconds.

The problem is that not all health information online is reliable. Websites can be difficult to navigate, use complex language, or provide incomplete, outdated, or inaccurate information.

item.title: Kuno cheetah cub dies of pellet injuries
item.description: It is the first killing of a cheetah since the wild animal was reintroduced in the country in 2022.
item.content:encoded:
A cheetah cub at Kuno National Park died from pellet injuries on Monday, a day after it was found wounded in the forests of Madhya Pradesh’s Morena district, The Indian Express reported.

Dr Shobha Jawre, from the College of Veterinary Science and Animal Husbandry in Jabalpur, confirmed to the newspaper that the 19-month-old male cub had died because of pellet injuries. “The pellets were removed from the cheetah cub’s body during an operation,” the doctor was quoted as saying.

A report has been submitted to the wildlife department.

It is the first killing, and the 25th death, of a cheetah since the wild animal was reintroduced in the country in 2022.

The cub was found injured by a monitoring team on Sunday in the Morena territorial forest division, the newspaper reported. The cub was taken to the veterinary institute in Jabalpur.

The State Tiger Strike Force, a wildlife crime investigation unit, is identifying persons responsible for the cheetah’s killing, The Indian Express reported.

The unit was focussing on a suspected poaching attempt besides human-animal conflict, the report added.

In September 2022, cheetahs from Namibia and South Africa were reintroduced to India seven decades after the species was declared extinct in the country.

item.title: Rage, lust and radical growth: Five must-read menopause novels
item.description: Terms like ‘meno-lit’ and ‘hot flush noir’ are surfacing – just as ‘chick-lit’ was once used to patronise commercial women’s fiction.
item.content:encoded:
Novels featuring older female characters enduring the joint horrors of ageism and misogyny have been around for a while. But fiction foregrounding the specifics of midlife hormonal changes is a surprisingly recent phenomenon.

Given the medical profiles of menopause (and its predecessor, perimenopause), perhaps it’s unsurprising that wellness guides and health-related memoirs have led the way.

Journalist Sam Baker’s pioneering The Shift, actor Naomi Watts’ Dare I Say It and Darcey Steinke’s Flash Count Diary combine personal experience with research. Handbooks like Liz Earle’s The Good Menopause Guide and Dr Mary Claire Havers’ series on perimenopause and menopause focus on disseminating facts.

Now that fiction is catching up, terms like “meno-lit” and “hot flush noir” are surfacing – just as “chick-lit” was once used to patronise commercial women’s fiction. Hopefully, the increasing visibility of menopausal protagonists will move past the novelty phase and become a mainstay of the novel. After all, the stages of menopause are a universal female experience. Surely, it’s time they were integrated into the wider realms of fiction.

Here are five novels tackling the early stages of menopause with fervour.

item.title: The seven crumbling pillars of India’s democracy
item.description: It is becoming painfully evident that the ailment affecting Indian democracy is not one that a change in government can cure.
item.content:encoded:
A century has passed since the publication of the autobiography of TE Lawrence, popularly known as Lawrence of Arabia. The title Seven Pillars of Wisdom is drawn from the Book of Proverbs in the Bible: “Wisdom hath builded her house, she hath hewn out her seven pillars.”

How appropriate, then, that in their wisdom, the founders of our Constitution went in for democracy as the form of government that would guide independent India’s destiny.

As it transpires, the structure of democracy in India rests on seven pillars, namely (i) legislature (ii) executive (political and bureaucratic) (iii) political parties (iv) judiciary (v) independent institutions (vi) media and (vii) civil society.

As of today, all the pillars appear shaky, threatening the future of democracy, although it could be argued that structural weaknesses in the Indian democratic edifice have existed right from 1947.

I Legislature

Let us start with the legislatures, both at the union and state levels. Cracks appeared in the post-Nehruvian era. The “aya Ram gaya Ram” phenomenon of politicians switching parties started in 1967, a legacy that continues to the present day. item.title: Cyclone Arnab: Over 89,000 evacuated, NDRF teams deployed ahead of Andhra landfall
item.description: More than 60 trains were cancelled as a precautionary measure as gusts of up to 150 km per hour were expected.
item.content:encoded:
Very severe cyclonic storm Arnab is expected to make landfall along the coast of Andhra Pradesh on Wednesday, the India Meteorological Department said on Tuesday.

The cyclone will make landfall between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam in Andhra Pradesh, close to Puducherry’s Yanam town, with the maximum sustained wind speed of 125 km per hour to 135 km per hour, gusting up to 150 km per hour, the weather department said. It is expected to make landfall in the early hours of Wednesday.

As of 2.30 pm Indian time on Tuesday, the cyclonic storm was centred about 170 km south of Vishakhapatnam.

Heavy rainfall

The cyclone will likely lead to isolated but extremely heavy rainfall in coastal Andhra Pradesh, Yanam, Odisha and Chhattisgarh on Tuesday and Wednesday, the weather department said.

It advised residents in these areas to remain alert, follow official weather updates and adhere to the advisories issued by the authorities.

Sea conditions will remain rough till at least Thursday morning, it added.

Relief measures

In Andhra Pradesh, nearly 89,000 persons living on the Kakinada coast were being shifted to relief camps, The Hindu reported.

Odisha was planning to shift 48,000 persons by Tuesday evening, PTI reported.

item.title: Queer short fiction: All kinds of adventures visit ‘Boy’, who works at a highway dhaba
item.description: An excerpt from ‘A Queer Shade of Saffron: Stories’, by Shastri Akella.
item.content:encoded:
The peepul lies flat on the ground, felled by a summer storm. Boy is sitting on its trunk again, waiting, when he sees a boy across the road, stepping in and out of the shadows of the leafy eucalyptus trees. Boy thinks of cream poured into a mug of coffee, disappearing, then rising again to the surface. He licks his lips, craving something sweet, and whistles. The boy, startled, looks up first, as if to spot the bird that’s the source of the sound. So, Boy whistles again. This time, the boy looks in his direction. Boy beckons him over. The boy runs across the road. Without breaking his stride, he leaps, pivots with a hand planted on the trunk, and lands next to Boy. Their shoulders touch, their heads are nearly level.

“What’s your name?” Boy asks. “Haven’t seen you before.”

“Madhu,” the boy replies. He tells Boy that he lived in Garhwal until the Ganga flooded his town and took his parents and Samosa the Dog. He sounds as if he’s reporting a loss endured by someone else; emotion doesn’t alter his voice or turn his eyes liquid.

item.description: The authorities had ordered him to exit the country by October 28, allegedly for participating in the protests against the chief election commissioner.
item.content:encoded:
The Bombay High Court on Tuesday put on hold the Leave India Notice issued to actor Imran Khan, The Indian Express reported.

The hearing was adjourned till Monday after the Union government said that no coercive action would be taken against Khan until then, Live Law reported.

On October 15, the Foreigners Regional Registration Office directed Khan, a citizen of the United States, to leave the country by October 28 allegedly for participating in the protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in Mumbai earlier this month.

A Leave India Notice is a directive issued by the authorities requiring a foreign citizen to exit the country within a specified time period. Failing to comply with the order could lead to detention, deportation or blacklisting.

Khan holds an Overseas Citizen of India card, which is an immigration status that allows foreign citizens of Indian origin to live and work in India indefinitely.

The actor had moved the High Court against the notice, with his lawyer saying that rules do not prohibit Overseas Citizen of India cardholders from participating in a protest.

Khan had been detained during the protest at the August Kranti Maidan in Mumbai on October 10.

item.title: SC seeks Centre’s reply on plea by media association against privacy law
item.description: The Digital News Publishers Association, which represents 21 news organisations, said that the Act ‘threatens’ journalistic activities.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday issued notice to the Union government seeking its response to a petition challenging the Digital Personal Data Protection Act and its rules, Bar and Bench reported.

The 2025 Digital Personal Data Protection Rules were notified by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology in November 2025, bringing into effect the 2023 Digital Personal Data Protection Act.

Section 44(3) of the Act imposes a blanket ban on the disclosure of personal information without defining what constitutes “personal information”.

The Digital News Publishers Association, which represents 21 media publishers, including those owned by businesspersons Mukesh Ambani and Gautam Adani, has challenged the law, citing violation of journalistic freedom, The Hindu reported.

The petition said that the law “threatens the full spectrum of journalistic activity carried out by journalists, ground reporters, citizens, whistleblowers, Right to Information activists and other stakeholders”, The Hindu reported.

The Act was contrary to the Supreme Court’s privacy judgement, which recognised the right to privacy as inviolable and fundamental to human dignity and life, the association contended.

The law “impermissibly restricts” the fundamental right to information, and freedom of speech and expression, the newspaper quoted the petition as saying.

The rules had clarified how organisations processing personal data should handle it, notify individuals of data breaches and obtain consent for data collection.

item.title: This book revisits the Buddha’s India teachings on living mindfully in the present, past, and future
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Touching the Footsteps of the Buddha’, by Thich Nhat Hanh, edited by Shantum Seth.
item.content:encoded:
To be in the here and in the now is the basic practice of Buddhism. We have talked about how in our daily life, our body may be at one place, but our mind is elsewhere. Our mind may be caught in the regret or sorrow concerning the past, or worries concerning the future. Often, we are locked into the prison of the past and are not able to live the present moment deeply.

But if you know how to bring your attention to your in-breath and breathe in mindfully, you will be able to release both the past and the future. If you bring your mind to the present, you will be able to release both the past and the future. In the Sutra on Mindful Breathing, the Buddha advises us to use that practice in order to become alive, and in order to release the tension and stress in our body.

item.title: Microsoft offers exit packages to 60,000 employees as it scales up AI investment
item.description: Around 30% of those eligible have already opted for the voluntary retirement plan.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees in India, Canada, the United States and the United Kingdom as the technology company increases its investments in artificial intelligence, AFP reported.

The latest offer covers about 27% of Microsoft’s global workforce.

Employees at the vice-president level and below were eligible for the offer. Some employees, including those working in data centres, sales and marketing, are excluded from the scheme. Around 30% of those eligible have already opted for the voluntary retirement plan, CNBC reported.

The company has been investing heavily in data centres to meet growing demand for AI computing and provide cloud services to companies including Anthropic and OpenAI.

Amy Coleman, an executive vice-president and chief people officer at Microsoft, said that the voluntary exit offer reflected the company’s efforts to adapt to changing business needs, the news agency reported.

“[We are] creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter,” AFP quoted Coleman as telling employees in a memo.

Microsoft had 2.23 lakh employees globally at the end of June, down from 2.28 lakh at the end of 2025, AFP reported, citing regulatory filings.

In July, the company cut nearly 5,000 jobs in its Xbox gaming division.

item.title: IISER Pune removes Umar Khalid’s book from library to ‘avoid misunderstanding or unrest’
item.description: The jailed activist’s book ‘Fractured Communities’ is based on his PhD thesis and examines the history of Adivasi societies in Jharkhand under British rule.
item.content:encoded:
A book by activist Umar Khalid has been removed from the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research Pune library to “avoid any misunderstanding or unrest”, The Indian Express quoted the administration as saying on Sunday.

Khalid has been in prison for more than six years without trial in connection with the 2020 Delhi riots conspiracy case.

The book, Fractured Communities: Adivasi Histories and the Politics of Power, was published earlier this year. It is based on Khalid’s PhD thesis at Jawaharlal Nehru University and examines the history of Adivasi societies in Singhbhum region of Jharkhand under British rule.

The book was removed after a social media account called Gems of Indian Academia shared a photograph showing it as a new addition to the institute’s library, The Indian Express reported.

Madabhushi Madan Gopal, chairperson of the institute’s board of governors, said on social media that he was “shocked” to learn that the book had been added to the library.

“This is retracted last night and action is initiated on those who played this mischief, I assure such things will not happen again in IISER Pune,” he said.

item.title: A documentary revisits Libia Lobo Sardesai’s remarkable contribution to the Goa liberation struggle
item.description: Anjali Monteiro and KP Jayasankar’s ‘Libby de Liberdade’ will be screened in Mumbai on October 30.
item.content:encoded:
Libia Lobo Sardesai is worthy of an international biopic, or a web series at the very least. It isn’t every day that you hear of a young woman who quit a secure job and co-founded an underground radio station to support Goa’s struggle to gain liberation from Portugal. Even rarer is the woman who gathered other achievements like some might pick flowers – a pioneering female lawyer, the founder of the Women’s Cooperative Bank in Goa as well as the Goa College of Home Science.

A recent documentary on Lobo Sardesai, who is now 102, gives some measure of her feats. Libby de Liberdade by Anjali Monteiro and KP Jayasankar is built around the creation of a mural to mark Lobo Sardesai’s birth centenary in 2024. Painted by Solomon Lobo, the grandson of the prominent artist Francis Newton Souza, the mural is situated right across from where Lobo Sardesai lives in Panaji.

The filmmakers also interview Lobo Sardesai at length, and include footage of various celebratory achievements around her. The 79-minute documentary will be screened on October 30 at Mumbai’s Prithvi Theatre by the Vikalp collective.

The demand by a special executive magistrate that student leader Neha Bora should furnish a peace bond of Rs 10,000 raises the uncomfortable question about whether the state is aiming to maintain public order or restrict dissent.

Peace bonds – legal promises to maintain public peace – are intended to prevent violence. But their use against protesters reiterates that in a democracy, the absence of protest is not proof of public peace.

Bora emphasised this in an article in The Indian Express on October 24. “What is this peace that I am being asked to maintain?” they asked. “...Is it the silence that follows when protesters have been dispersed, detained or frightened into staying home? item.title: As Adani files defamation case, Calcutta HC blocks sharing of video about alleged ties with Modi

The Calcutta High Court on Monday barred the publication, uploading and sharing of a documentary about the alleged close ties between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and industrialist Gautam Adani until January 31.

The order came after Adani Enterprises Limited filed a Rs 50 crore defamation suit against tech entrepreneur Sabeer Bhatia and others, seeking to stop the circulation of the 36-minute video, The Friendship Files: How Modi and Adani Stole India.

The video was uploaded on October 9 on Bhatia’s YouTube channel and was also posted on X.

Justice Aryak Dutt said that the documentary was not a news report. He added that the allegations made in the video were not substantiated by any authority.

The court described the documentary as a dramatised narrative whose title “insinuates theft” and whose narration and visuals were presented as factual.

“Constructive criticism or truthful reporting on the petitioner or on government policy, backed by evidence, is not barred,” the court said.

The original video had already been disabled, but Bhatia uploaded it again, the court noted. It said this prima facie showed “want of good faith”.

item.title: Memoir: A searing account of growing up in a family shaped by bipolar disorder and inheriting it
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Traitor in the House: My Bipolar Life’, by Shubha Menon.
item.content:encoded:
My mother suffered from bipolar disorder. We didn’t have a name for the illness but we experienced its effects in bizarre ways. One late evening, as I sat doing my homework, my mother came into the room, agitated and manic. She ordered me to get up and follow her to the terrace. She said that I had no redeeming qualities, nothing going for me, nothing to live for. It would be best if I jumped off the roof with her.

I should not be afraid, she said, because we would hold hands. When I tried to run away, she threw me on the ground and pummelled my chest with her bare feet. My brother and sister heard my yelling and rescued me.

The incident left an indelible mark on me. I became quiet, moving around the house invisibly, trying to ensure that I didn’t see or hear my mother, and more importantly, that she didn’t see or hear me. But I was marked – or should I say marred – for life.

item.title: How children with disabilities are made to jump through hoops to access benefits
item.description: They need a unique ID number to avail of a range of benefits, including a disability pension. The process of getting one can take years.
item.content:encoded:
Sangeeta Prajapati applied for a Unique Disability Identity number for her 14-year-old daughter, Om Kumari, in April 2025. Since then, she has spent at least five nights at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences in South Delhi, seeking appointments with specialist doctors to assess Kumari, who has autism.

The assessments are the most important steps in the generation of the UDID number. In Kumari’s case, doctors need to evaluate her reasoning, learning and problem-solving capabilities, as well as her adaptive behaviour, which covers a range of social skills, and skills required for activities of daily living. Additionally, Kumari will also need to be screened for associated comorbidities pertaining to hearing, visual or locomotor impairments.

Hospitals carry out the assessments for persons with autism, intellectual disability and cerebral palsy over a series of sessions. They issue an appointment for each session separately. “I get a message from the hospital to collect the token for a doctor to see Om,” said Prajapati. So far, she has received the message five times, asking her to be present the following day. item.title: Lula’s ‘miracle’ victory buys time for Brazil, resonates globally amid rise of far-right
item.description: The world’s fourth-largest democracy has now bucked the trend of far-right gains, and is a symbol that democrats elsewhere will not ignore.
item.content:encoded:
Three weeks ago, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s political obituaries had all been written.

The far-right presidential candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro, had come out of the first round of the presidential election with a lead that looked impossible to overcome.

At 80 years old, Lula seemed headed for a quiet exit after four decades at the centre of Brazilian political life.

On Sunday, however, Lula proved everyone wrong. He won the runoff and secured a fourth non-consecutive term as Brazil’s president.

A night of firsts

The election result is unprecedented in Brazilian politics in at least three ways.

First, no Brazilian presidential candidate had ever won the first round and then lost the runoff. Since the two-round system was adopted by the 1988 Brazilian Constitution, the first-round leader had always gone on to win.

Lula broke that pattern by turning a defeat of around 2.2 million votes in the first round into a solid victory, in three weeks.

Second, no Brazilian president has ever been elected to four terms. When his new term ends, Lula will have governed Brazil for 16 (non-consecutive) years – the longest democratically elected tenure in the country’s history.

item.title: This novel in verse tells the legend of Unniarcha, Kerala’s most fearless Kalaripayattu warrior girl
item.description: An excerpt from ‘I Am Archa’, by Ranjeeta Raam.
item.content:encoded:
Kalaripayattu

is an art.
is warfare.
is a way of living.
is in my blood.
is all I have ever known.
is Kannappa Chekavar.

Kannappa Chekavar

is my acha,
my father.

He is disciplined and strict.
He is loving and encouraging too.

He is also the greatest
Kalari master of Kadathanadu.

He is unmatchable,
unbeatable
in this art of war
fought with every weapon used in close combat.
Wooden staffs, swords, daggers, maces
are mere toys in his hands.

It is said he knows more adavukkal – combat moves –
than anyone else practising Kalaripayattu.
It is also said
that he has never taught
all nineteen of them to anyone.

He has shared all
but the last technique,
the most cunning one,
keeping it close to his heart,
waiting for that special student
worthy enough to earn this secret.

No pity

The consequence of being ten minutes late
is an extra hour of practice.

Breathless and exhausted,
I gaze longingly
at the other students leaving the class.
They must be off to the vacant field
by the village pond
to hang out and play
before the sun sets for the day.

Aromal steps out too,
casting a look of disappointment
in my direction.

Control your breathing, Unniarcha!
Acha interrupts my thoughts.
No pity, no sympathy in that voice.
Sigh!

Agony

Without a word,
I continue practising the chuvadukkal –
the basic steps and foot placements,
into the second hour.

like the summer rainstorm outside.

item.title: Centre amends rules to allow E100 fuel in compatible vehicles
item.description: The modified rules allow flex-fuel vehicles to run on nearly 100% ethanol, alongside E85, which contains 85% ethanol and 15% petrol.
item.content:encoded:
The Union government has amended rules to allow vehicles designed for flex-fuel to run on E100, a fuel made up of nearly 100% ethanol.

The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways issued the notification amending the Motor Vehicles Rules on Friday. The changes came into effect on Monday.

The modified rules allow flex-fuel vehicles to run on E100 alongside E85, which contains 85% ethanol and 15% petrol.

Flex-fuel vehicles can run on different blends of petrol and ethanol. However, regular petrol vehicles, including those designed to run on E20 fuel, which contains 20% ethanol and 80% petrol, cannot use E85 or E100, Hindustan Times reported.

Under its Ethanol Blended Petrol programme, the government mandates that all petrol sold in the country be blended with 20% ethanol – a substance produced from sugarcane and food grain. The policy is aimed at reducing India’s dependency on fossil fuels, cutting greenhouse gas emissions and boosting income for sugarcane farmers.

However, consumers have complained that the new fuel mix damages engines and reduces their mileage.

An opinion poll by LocalCircles published on July 5 showed that 53% of the surveyed petrol vehicle owners said that they believe that the government’s handling of the E20 rollout was “disastrous” or “ineffective”.

item.title: Seven foreigners in terror-related probe get bail yet Indian undertrials struggle to access rights
item.description: The broader concern is the protections in law are unevenly accessible.
item.content:encoded:
A Delhi Special Court’s decision to allow seven foreign nationals under National Investigation Agency investigation in a terrorism-related case to travel home for a month raises a constitutional question: how should criminal law balance national security, investigative deadlines and personal liberty?

The accused, an American national, Matthew Aaron VanDyke and six Ukrainian citizens were arrested in March 2026. The allegations included drone assembly, electronic warfare training and support to ethnic armed organisations along the Indo-Myanmar border.

However, after the statutory period for filing a chargesheet expired, the NIA’s report omitted substantive charges under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, and instead cited regulatory violations under the Foreigners Act, 1946. The agency maintained that its wider investigation into scheduled terrorism offences continued.

The Special Court for the NIA at Rouse Avenue, New Delhi, granted default bail and later allowed the accused to travel abroad, subject to personal bonds and diplomatic undertakings. They did not decide the merits of the allegations or represent judicial leniency; they enforced a statutory deadline. The central question is not why these foreign nationals secured release, but why comparable safeguards remain difficult for many Indian undertrials to exercise.

The court also issued notice to the Election Commission, while refusing to pass an interim order extending the deadline for filing claims and objections or restraining the poll panel from publishing the final electoral roll.

item.title: Karnataka poll officials sought deletions of 61,000 voters without citing reasons: ‘The Hindu’
item.description: The officials said that the Form 7 applications were ‘auto-generated’ with their digital signatures amid the special intensive revision of electoral rolls.
item.content:encoded:
Election officials filed 61,059 Form 7 applications seeking to remove voters from Karnataka’s electoral rolls without stating any reason during the special intensive revision, The Hindu reported on Monday.

The 1960 Registration of Electors Rules mandate that an application to delete voters should be rejected if it does not state the reason for the request.

In the case of Karnataka, electoral registration officers and assistant electoral registration officers said that the system “auto-generated” these forms and added their digital signatures when voters could not be reached during hearings of notices issued for no mapping or “logical discrepancies”, reported The Hindu.

In such cases, voters were marked as “ineligible”.

“Logical discrepancies” flagged by the poll panel during the voter list revision included mismatches in parents’ names, low age gap with parents and the number of children of the parents being above six.

The officials said that they had been instructed to file Form 7 applications if a voter had moved, had a duplicate entry elsewhere, was underage, had died or was not an Indian citizen, The Hindu reported. However, since the forms were auto-generated, the reason for seeking deletion was left blank.

item.description: The Congress leader’s statement that the home minister was a ‘murder accused’ was not defamatory, the court held.
item.content:encoded:
A court in Uttar Pradesh’s Sultanpur on Monday acquitted Congress leader Rahul Gandhi in a criminal defamation case over his 2018 remarks referring to Union Home Minister Amit Shah as a “murder accused”, Bar and Bench reported.

Gandhi was present in court when Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate Shubham Verma pronounced the verdict. The court said the remarks were not defamatory in nature.

The case was filed in August 2018 on a complaint by Bharatiya Janata Party leader Vijay Mishra, who alleged that Gandhi had made objectionable remarks about Shah at a press conference in Bengaluru on May 8, 2018, during the Karnataka elections. Shah was the BJP’s national president at the time.

Gandhi had said that the BJP claimed to believe in clean politics but had a party president who was a “murder accused”, in an apparent reference to the 2005 Sohrabuddin Sheikh case.

Sohrabuddin Sheikh, who was a wanted criminal, was killed by the Gujarat Police in November 2005 in an “encounter”, which is alleged to have been staged. Some vehicles in Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s convoy met with an accident on the Purvanchal Expressway in Uttar Pradesh at around 10.15 am on Monday while he was travelling from Lucknow to Sultanpur for a court hearing in a defamation case, PTI reported.

Sultanpur Superintendent of Police Vineet Jaiswal said no one was injured, The Indian Express reported.

Media reports had initially said that several persons were injured.

Gandhi was travelling to Sultanpur to appear before a special MP-MLA court in connection with a 2018 defamation case for his remarks about Union Home Minister Amit Shah. He has been acquitted in the matter.

The incident occurred when a private vehicle at the front of the convoy, reportedly belonging to a Congress leader, applied the brakes suddenly for an unspecified reason, causing vehicles behind it to collide, a police officer told PTI.

The vehicles involved had joined the convoy midway. Congress workers from neighbouring districts were travelling in them.

The Uttar Pradesh Police has formed a special investigation team to probe what led to the accident and determine whether there were any lapses in security, escort arrangements or traffic management, PTI reported.

item.title: Rising pollution: India has dashboards to track problem – but not to track capability to solve it
item.description: Measuring policy outcomes has become more efficient than examining whether capability in providing public services has actually improved.

On October 21, Delhi’s air quality slipped into the “poor” category, prompting the Commission for Air Quality Management to invoke Stage I of the Graded Response Action Plan across the National Capital Region.

This stage involves measures such as intensifying the mechanical sweeping roads and sprinkling water on them to keep the dust from rising. It also bans some kinds of construction and demolition activities.

As winter progresses, the air quality in the capital is likely to deteriorate further. Pollution-control measures will be activated, agencies will issue advisories, monitoring stations will track concentrations and dashboards will show the public how air quality is changing.

There is no shortage of information about Delhi’s air. A 2019 review of five emission-inventory studies by the Council on Energy, Environment and Water found that transport accounted for roughly 18% to 39% of PM2.5 emissions and road dust for 18% to 38%, while road dust alone accounted for 36% to 66% of PM10.

item.title: In a new book, Gopalkrishna Gandhi studies his grandfather Mahatma Gandhi’s views on Hinduism
item.description: ‘Whenever there is distress which one cannot remove, one must fast and pray.’
item.content:encoded:
“My religion teaches me that whenever there is distress which one cannot remove, one must fast and pray.”

India has had a tradition of fasting as a means of self-denial, self-purification, and self-mortification. This is an integral part of India’s religious and cultural history. Fasting on certain given days of the month and week, and on certain days connected with epic lore, such as on Mahashivaratri, makes fasts more than integral to Hinduism; it makes them vital and essential to it. In the Jaina tradition, fasting is even higher in the order of observances, as in Gandhi’s description of his Jain-influenced mother fasting unfailingly and cheerfully, having been seen earlier in this narrative. And Indian Muslims, of course, observe the annual fasts in the month of Ramzan punctiliously, Gandhi noting the practice with admiration in his illustrious colleague, Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan.

Gandhi himself belonged very squarely to that tradition, the reasons for his fasts varying, but the mode remaining very Hindu-Jaina, very religious in its DNA. item.title: Uttar Pradesh: EC orders reverification of voter roll entries made by computer operators after SIR
item.description: This came after the Congress alleged that names of over 13,000 voters were replaced with those of other persons after the publication of final list in Pilibhit.
item.content:encoded:
The Election Commission on Sunday ordered the reverification of all names added to, deleted from or amended in Uttar Pradesh’s electoral rolls through Forms 6, 7 and 8 by computer assistants in all 403 Assembly constituencies after the special intensive revision ended on April 10, the Hindustan Times reported.

The forms are used to register new voters, delete names and correct entries.

item.title: A new Brahmin-first party in UP symbolises a growing disquiet among BJP’s core voters

Since February this year, an office space in Lucknow’s Sapru Marg has become the home of an audacious political experiment. Every day, a handful of men gather here and brainstorm how they can subvert the Bharatiya Janata Party in the upcoming assembly elections in Uttar Pradesh.

Curiously, the men admit to having been BJP voters all their lives. They are mostly Brahmins, the privileged caste group that is a core constituency of the Hindutva party.

“The BJP was our party,” says Rajesh Shukla, a businessman who is a regular visitor here. “It has now been hijacked by backwards.”

The businessman was referring to other backward classes, or OBCs, a collection of castes that make up nearly half of UP’s population. Traditionally, the BJP has been seen as a party catering to upper-caste Hindus. Its earliest political architects like Deendayal Upadhyaya, Atal Bihari Vajpayee and Murli Manohar Joshi were Brahmins from UP.

However, over the past decade, it has won two consecutive state elections after successfully wooing OBC and Scheduled Caste voters.

item.title: Why rats are on the ballot in Canada’s civic elections
item.description: Rodents point to broader societal concerns about housing, public services and civic engagement.
item.content:encoded:
Rats are on the ballot in Canadian municipal elections this fall, with several political parties promising to tackle city rat problems. While rats may seem like a niche election issue, they can point to broader societal concerns about housing, public services and civic engagement.

Rats are ubiquitous urban residents that cities have attempted to evict for centuries. Often portrayed as dirty pests and bringers of plague, they can harbour pathogens that cause illnesses to people and pets, like rat bite fever and leptospirosis.

So why have cities had so little success in reducing rat numbers?

Well, rats are synanthropes, species that benefit from living alongside humans, and have adapted remarkably well to our paved, cacophonic and bustling streets. Cities provide abundant resources for rats to thrive: food scraps are meals; standing water on sidewalks supplies drinking water; and cracks in buildings offer access to shelter.

Municipal policies and bylaws shape how these environments are built and maintained, influencing living conditions for both people and rats. Thinking about rats through municipal elections can offer a more tangible way to understand how complex it is to manage rats without addressing broader issues.

item.description: Sri Lanka’s capital has a severe paucity of crucial public hygiene facilities, with women bearing the brunt of this neglect.

“Menstruating monthly is not an illness,” says Sumithra Randenigala, who works as a security guard in Sri Lanka’s largest city, Colombo. But when she has her monthly period, the 26-year-old often calls in sick to work.

Getting her pay docked some days each month is a better alternative than being unable to use the toilet during the two-hour daily train commute from her sleepy seaside town Bentota to Colombo Fort Station.

“If I need to change my pad, the toilet on the train is locked or blocked. At work, guards aren’t allowed to use the office toilet,” she tells me at the Sri Lanka Tea Board, where she works.

She attended school till age 14, where she learnt about urinary tract infections in class. She knows the importance of changing her sanitary pad frequently. After several painful experiences of contracting UTIs, she now chooses to forfeit her daily pay sometimes, rather than risk an infection that would force her to take a week of unpaid sick leave.

item.title: How the British looted Indian property after the uprising of 1857 – and justified it
item.description: In diaries and written accounts, English officers and wives cheer on the plunder of Indian belongings as retribution and revenge for violence by sepoys.
item.content:encoded:
Crockery from the Awadh palace. Silver items and animals from Nana Saheb Peshwa’s Bithur palace. Ornaments and silk garments belonging to Mughal Emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar. These were among the items looted by the British during the uprising of 1857.

But looting, it seems from books written by British men and women who experienced the rebellion, was only what violent Indians did. Their accounts present a rather different framing of the marauding. Their descriptions of the plunder by the British suggest that they were heroes who were merely rectifying an unfortunate mistake.

Even as they expressed a fear of their belongings falling into Indian hands, British writers also describe indulging in the plunder and destruction of Indian property and cheering it on – despite a proclamation from the East India Company authorities forbidding this.

They did so with impunity, fearing neither social ostracisation nor judicial repercussions.

‘All we valued was lost to us…’

When the uprising began in Meerut on May 10, 1857, the looting was incidental since the focus of the sepoys of the East India Company was to punish their British officers.

But Delhi, where the sepoys went next, witnessed large-scale looting.

item.title: As Brazil votes again, Lula remains a crucial bulwark against Trump in the region
item.description: A victory for Flávio Bolsonaro on October 25 will lead to Brazil aligning closely with US security and economic interests.
item.content:encoded:
On October 25, Brazilians will return to the polls for the second round of the presidential election. The results will matter not only for the future of country itself, but also for the region and the world.

Alongside Canada and Mexico, Brazil, under the leadership of current President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, is one of the few countries in the region that has stood up to Donald Trump’s meddling and interference attempts.

The rise of the far right

Under Lula, Brazil still serves as a bulwark against the imposition of right-wing populist agendas critics say run counter to the broader interests of local societies, but cater to the interests of certain domestic elites. It is within this context that we must consider the Brazilian election alongside other electoral processes in the democratic world.

As Wikipedia notes, Almora is a municipal town and cantonment in Uttarakhand’s Kumaun region. It did not emerge from the pressures of recent urbanisation. Rather, it is a 600-year-old town situated on the Kashyap Hills. It sits on a 5-km-long mountain ridge that forms a distinct horseshoe shape.

Indeed, Almora is older than Kolkata, Chennai or Mumbai.

During the late 16th century, the Chanda rulers of Kali Kumaon (today’s Champawat) shifted their capital to Almora, which, in certain accounts, was referred to as Alamnagar. This is how the town is believed to have been founded. It later passed into the hands of the Gorkhas for a brief period and became part of British India in 1816, following the formalisation of the Treaty of Sugauli between the British and the Gorkhas.

Beyond this ruler-oriented history, Almora has a rich past of its own. Hailed as the cultural capital of Kumaun, it encompasses linguistic, literary, and spiritual history that give it the life of a thriving town.

item.title: As memories become entangled with machines, who controls what we remember?
item.description: History could now be determined by algorithms.
item.content:encoded:
My phone chimed with an automated “memory” slideshow from an old trip, set to gentle music, the skies impossibly blue, the faces so bright. I watched it twice before realising what bothered me: I hadn’t chosen the photos, the order, or the mood. Something else had decreed what my holiday felt like. If the machine had the sky wrong, would I know? Is a memory still mine once something else has contrived it?

But how reliable are our memories anyway? Elizabeth Loftus, a pioneer in false memory research, proved decades ago that a single leading question can rewrite our recollections. Today, experts know that memory is actively rebuilt every time we remember.

The act of offloading memory onto external tools – like a simple notebook – blurs the line between the mind and the environment. This phenomenon, described as the “extended mind” by philosophers Andy Clark and David Chalmers, finds a modern parallel in media theory through the concepts of mediatisation and mediation, where historical reality is consumed in a pre-edited format.

Was the holocaust the great aberration of this dream? Believers in the Enlightenment idea – which continues to define modernity worldwide – would say so: a devastating violation.

item.title: A critical flaw in PHP, ‘backbone of the web’, has cyber experts scrambling for a fix
item.description: The incident shows that vulnerabilities will recur as long as the world treats open-source foundational tools charity rather than critical security investment.

Details have been published of a critical flaw in the programming language PHP, which is the backbone of more than 70% of all websites. Left unfixed, the flaw would allow hackers to easily take over and compromise millions of websites and the information held on their servers. In response, multiple European governments and operators including the Port of Rotterdam have taken websites offline.

The Australian Signals Directorate, America’s Cyber Defence Agency, and similar bodies from the United Kingdom, Europe and Japan have all warned web developers to apply urgent updates to their core systems, and to consider taking down websites until safety can be guaranteed.

item.title: Opinion: India should welcome Musk’s Starlink – but ensure that it holds the switch

The Delhi Police has granted permission for singer Diljit Dosanjh’s concert at the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium on October 30, IANS quoted the event’s ticketing partner BookMyShow as saying on Friday.

This came a day after the police denied clearance for the event because of threat-related inputs and security requirements during the festive season.

The Hindu festival of Diwali will be celebrated on November 8.

On Friday, BookMyShow clarified that any media reports claiming that the concert had been cancelled were inaccurate.

“Permission for the event had been temporarily withheld, not cancelled, and the two should not be confused,” IANS quoted the platform as saying.

It added that the police had asked the concert’s organisers and BookMyShow to ensure additional safety and traffic management measures.

“BookMyShow Live had a cordial meeting with Delhi Police, presented a detailed plan and have assured Delhi Police of full compliance with all security/traffic requirements,” said the ticketing platform.

It added: “On that basis, permission for the event has been reconsidered and issued.”

After Delhi, Dosanjh is scheduled to perform in Indore, Ahmedabad, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Lucknow and Chandigarh in November and December as part of his Aura India Tour.

item.title: From a new compilation of tales from mythology and folklore: Vasishtha looks for a place to meditate
item.description: An excerpt from ‘The Blue Lotus: Myths and Folk Tales of India’, by Meena Arora Nayak.
item.content:encoded:
Seeking to detach himself from the world, Rishi Vasishtha looked for a place where he could meditate in seclusion – a place without the distractions of the city, forest, sky, ocean, clouds, creatures, gods, or souls. He found a spot in space that was so far away from earth that even the natural elements could not reach it. In that empty place, he imagined a small hermitage and made it inaccessible to the rest of the world. Then he sat down in it in the lotus posture, and quietening his mind, went into samadhi for a hundred years.

On awakening, when he willed his consciousness to return, he heard a sigh. In this place of his imagination, which was so far away in empty space, where not even air could intrude, he wondered where that sound was coming from, and from whom. So he went back into the infinite consciousness of his mind and began searching. In his mind were order and disorder and countless universes in different stages of creation and destruction. item.description: The demonstration was called by the Delhi Coordination Committee of People Against SIR – a civil society group consisting of students, farmers and activists.

The Delhi Police on Friday detained several protesters as they attempted to march to the Election Commission headquarters to demand Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation for his handling of the special intensive revision of electoral rolls.

The march had been called by the Delhi Coordination Committee of People Against SIR – a civil society group consisting of students, farmers and rights activists. They were joined by Communist Party of India (Marxist) leader Brinda Karat, members of the All India Democratic Women’s Association and the All India Democratic Students’ Organisation.

The demonstration began near Gole Dak Khana in central Delhi, with the protesters shouting slogans against Kumar and calling for a halt to the voter roll revision.

More than 13 crore names have been removed from the draft electoral rolls across 30 states and Union territories during the exercise.

item.title: SBI says it informed customers after details of nearly 3,900 account holders leaked in cyberattack
item.description: Around 3.75 lakh customer records were released on the dark web, of which 3,897 contained personally identifiable information.
item.content:encoded:
The State Bank of India on Friday said it had individually informed customers whose personal data was leaked on the dark web following a cyberattack, using email or WhatsApp.

The cyberattack on Wednesday had led to the leak of about 3.75 lakh customer records on the dark web, of which 3,897 contained personally identifiable information.

The bank’s statement came after digital rights organisation Internet Freedom Foundation flagged that SBI had informed stock exchanges about the data leak but had not notified affected customers.

In its statement on Friday, the SBI said that customers’ account balances and funds were safe. “Customers are advised to follow safe digital banking practices, never share their OTP, PIN or password with anyone, and remain vigilant against suspicious calls, messages and emails,” it added.

In July, customer data and internal documents from state-run Bank of Baroda were also leaked on the dark web, Reuters reported.

The Reserve Bank of India has repeatedly warned lenders about cybersecurity risks that could affect financial stability.

item.title: Uttar Pradesh: ‘Irregularities’ found in over 10,000 entries to Pilibhit electoral rolls
item.description: The Bharatiya Janata Party had won the seat by a margin of less than 7,000 votes in the 2022 Assembly polls.
item.content:encoded:
“Irregularities” have been found in 10,470 entries in the electoral roll of the Pilibhit Assembly constituency after the special intensive revision, said the Uttar Pradesh Chief Electoral Officer Navdeep Rinwa on Thursday.

Rinwa also announced that legal action will be taken against the current and former electoral registration officers in the constituency, while the services of a computer assistant at the Voter Registration Centre of Pilibhit will be terminated.

The action was taken after an investigation by the Pilibhit district election officer showed that the computer assistant had entered 13,779 Form 8 applications.

Form 8 is meant for shifting residence and correcting details in an existing electoral roll.

“No forms or records related to any of these entries were found available in the office,” said the chief election officer.

He added that of the total, 10,470 forms for “corrections” were approved. Irregularities were found in all of them, said Rinwa.

The statement came a day after the Congress alleged that the names of more than 13,000 voters were replaced with those of other persons after the final electoral list was released in April following the special intensive revision.

The voter identity card numbers and serial numbers of these voters had remained the same, said the party.

item.title: ‘Gajab Raat’ review: Manoj Bajpayee fires up a thriller that runs out of steam
item.description: Ritesh Shah’s Hindi thriller, co-written with Neeraj Pandey, is out on Netflix.
item.content:encoded:
In 2023, Manoj Bajpayee headlined the aptly titled film Sirf Ek Bandaa Kaafi Hai, playing a lawyer who refuses to come under pressure for representing a rape survivor. All it takes is one unwavering man – Bajpayee has come to embody this dogged, obdurate and cussed person, who acts as he pleases and moves sidewinder-like towards justice. Gajab Raat needs exactly such a person.

Ritesh Shah’s Hindi film, co-written with and produced by Neeraj Pandey, stars Bajpayee as Ajay, a lowly Delhi Police inspector who finds himself in charge of a knotty case. A grievously injured young woman has been found lying on a street in Delhi. Her identity is a mystery.

Several important people want to get to her, including social worker Neha (Shraddha Das), the Central Bureau of Investigation’s Madhok (Akshay Oberoi) and the National Investigation Agency’s Karan (Saqib Saleem). They have to get past Ajay, who creates a Great Wall-like barrier with not entirely altruistic motives.

Ajay has a reputation for selling out to the highest bidder. The latest case will prove whether Ajay is a sell-out or a hero.

The cast includes Rajiv Gupta as Ajay’s senior officer, Kiku Sharda as a hotel owner and Nushrratt Bharuccha as one of Ajay’s special friends.

item.title: Brand story: How entrepreneur MP Ramachandran made Ujala fabric whitener a laundry bestseller
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Brief Case: How Brands Create Desire, Trust and Culture’, by Sanjay Arora.
item.content:encoded:
Most problems that change the world don’t look like problems at all.

They look like mild inconveniences, the kind of thing most people shrug off and live with.

MP Ramachandran couldn’t shrug it off. He was obsessed with white clothes, wore only white shirts, washed them himself and was perpetually dissatisfied with the result. The whites faded, they yellowed, they looked like they’d given up. And every fabric whitener on the market made the problem worse rather than better.

Most people would have bought a different shirt.

Ramachandran built a company.


MP Ramachandran was not a typical entrepreneur. He was an accountant working in Mumbai who wore only white. His biggest frustration was that whites never stayed that way, they faded quickly, stains showed more easily and they looked old and ragged faster than coloured clothes.

That frustration became the catalyst.

Robin Blue was the dominant player in fabric whiteners at the time. But the problem with these powders was the process: consumers had to manually dissolve the powder, strain it through cloth and hope it didn’t leave blue patches on the fabric. Messy, unreliable and it still didn’t deliver the whiteness it promised.

item.title: FDA suspends licences of 8 Mumbai eateries, seizes 38 tonnes of food stock in Maharashtra
item.description: The establishments whose permits were held include You Mee in Ghatkopar and a Domino’s Pizza outlet in Bhandup.
item.content:encoded:
The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration suspended the licences of eight eateries in Mumbai and seized nearly 38 tonnes of food stock worth Rs 54.6 lakh across the state during inspections on Wednesday and Thursday.

The inspections uncovered violations, including unhygienic kitchens and drainage systems, rusted racks and utensils, incomplete temperature records, workers without medical certificates and the use of unauthorised food colours in sweets.

The establishments whose licences were suspended in Mumbai are SK Bakery in Mazgaon, Nekzad Restaurant in Grant Road, Foodies Multi Cuisine in Bandra, Arabian Luqma in Jogeshwari and Delhi Zaika in Kurla. The list also includes You Mee in Ghatkopar, a Domino’s Pizza outlet in Bhandup and Bikkgane Biryani in Govandi-Chembur.

The Food and Drug Administration said that the licences had been suspended with immediate effect. However, it did not specify which violations were found at each establishment.

As for the seizures, the largest was reported in Navi Mumbai, where officials confiscated 33,286 kg of kidney beans and other pulses worth about Rs 50 lakh from RDC Agro Ventures in the Shirwane area of Nerul.

The department said that the products were suspected to be substandard and incorrectly labelled.

item.description: Ayushmann Khurrana leads Akash A Kaushik’s film.

For all those wondering whether there is anything left to say about spies on lengthy missions in hostile territory after Dhurandhar, here is Udta Teer. In Akash A Kaushik’s Hindi-language comedy, the situation is reversed: a Pakistani agent has worked his way up to the top of India’s counter-terrorism unit.

Bilal (Ayushmann Khurrana), who is passing himself off as Vikrant, is not only his agency’s top operative but also a family man – his wife Yamini (Sara Ali Khan) is in the Defence ministry. When Bilal’s boss Burman (Rahul Bose) suspects that there is a mole in his office, he asks Bilal to investigate. Such is the trust that Bilal commands.

Alas, Bilal is scheming away in the shadows along with a couple of other undercover Pakistanis. Bilal arranges the escape of Pakistani terrorist Maqsood (Mukul Dev) but then loses his memory.

Bilal wakes up as Vikrant, confused about which country he is supposed to protect. Bilal is now a true-blue Indian patriot, who prays in a Hindu temple with gusto and goes after Maqsood with a vengeance.

item.title: Review: ‘Magazine’ is at a loose end, like its Gen Z hero
item.description: Shubham Shevade’s Marathi film, starring Raghav Vartak, is out in cinemas.
item.content:encoded:
Velu is bored, listless and confused about his future. The affluent and coddled young man fits some stereotypes about Gen Z, especially when he grandly “resigns” from a magazine published by his father after being scoffed at for wanting to explore “conflict”.

In search of inspiration and direction, Velu (Raghav Vartak) takes off for his father’s sugarcane farm in his ancestral village of Dattawad. Velu’s roseate memories of Dattawad are somewhat at odds with its present. Nothing much has changed here, Velu marvels – something his childhood friends Shripadh (Sudarshan Deshmukh) and Pushkar (Nilesh Mane) do not entirely agree with.

Magazine, which is out in cinemas, wants to pursue a back-to-roots story that is complicated by reality. Shubham Sanjay Shevade’s Marathi-language drama, co-written with Prateek Handore, is big on flashbacks, montages and scenes built around unstructured conversations as Velu tries to find his footing.

item.title: Review: ‘Doosra’ tries to force-fit two incompatible ideas
item.description: Abhinay Deo’s film is a hybrid between documentary and fiction, with a starring role for Sourav Ganguly.
item.content:encoded:
Abhinay Deo’s Doosra refers to, all at once, the delivery style in cricket, the endeavour of the story’s heroine to seek an alternative to her miserable life and the film’s hybrid form. Doosra is part-documentary and part-fictional feature, in which former Indian captain Sourav Ganguly fires the imagination of a cricket-loving woman in a small town.

The story unfolds between 1991 and 2002. Tara (Plabita Borthakur) belongs to a conservative family in which women are expected to know their place. When Tara speaks up, she is slapped by her strict father (Ankur Vikal). Elsewhere, the Indian cricket team is getting beaten up too, as is the country itself.

In unsure times, amidst a balance of payments crisis and a cricket betting scandal, Sourav Ganguly stands for much-needed chutzpah, his reputation for arrogance and his refusal to take orders just what the country’s battered image needs, according to Doosra. item.title: Review: ‘Tu Hai Meri Kiran’ puts a twist on stalking
item.description: Karan Rawal’s thriller stars Sonakshi Sinha, Zaheer Iqbal and Ankit Gupta.
item.content:encoded:
Tu Hai Meri Kiran gets its title from the song of the same name in Darr (1993), about a deranged man who harasses the woman with whom he is obsessed. Karan Rawal’s film, which is out in cinemas, gives stalking an intriguing, and absorbing, twist.

Kiran (Sonakshi Sinha) finds an old flip phone in her house in Mussoorie that connects her to Samar (Zaheer Iqbal). Kiran is a writer struggling to complete her second novel, and is married to Riyaan (Ankit Gupta). Samar, troubled and in trouble for his noxious behaviour, will prove to be a handful for Kiran.

Rawal’s screenplay, which borrows its major idea from a Korean show, is laden with suspense. The least twisty aspect of Tu Hai Meri Kiran is that stalking behaviour, which is condoned by the euphemism “one-sided love”, has frightening staying power. This idea gives a tinge of horror to Karan Rawal’s screenplay, despite strenuous efforts to humanise Samar and give him a tear-jerking back story.

Rawal admirably maintains an air of tension across 125 minutes. Some willing suspension of disbelief is necessary to go along with the film’s conceit. item.title: Why India needs citizen-centric governance for everyday democracy
item.description: Significant effort is required to extract even basic accountability from the state.
item.content:encoded:
In recent months, young Indians have felt compelled to petition, protest, run aggressive social media campaigns and push back against the government’s business-as-usual approach to irregularities in the manner in which electoral lists are being revised and in the way examinations are being conducted.

These protests reflect a wider frustration with the lack of avenues for citizens to engage with and hold accountable the governments and representatives they elect across levels.

Between the five-year election cycles, citizens have few systemic avenues to engage with their elected leaders and governments, contribute to decision-making, track commitments and projects or seek remedial action.

When the state fails to offer meaningful platforms for engagement and accountability, people are left with no options but to resort to protests on matters as basic as access to drinking water, quality education, health care or pothole-free roads or obstacle-free footpaths or fair examinations and recruitment to government services.
